# 035 · A NaN check written as == Float.NaN never fires, and fcmpl quietly becomes fcmpg

[← All examples](../README.md)

| Verdict | Categories | Severity if shipped | Change | Verified unit | Approach |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **✗ Violation: counterexample found** | functional | high | cleanup, behaviour change not intended | [`Comparison#fcmp`](../../examples/apps/mica/src/main/java/net/terminalvalue/mica/interp/Comparison.java) | [B9: Regression verification](../../lib/README.md) |

> The interpreter's `fcmp` implements `fcmpg` and `fcmpl` with four branches: less, greater, equal, and the unordered case that the two opcodes decide differently. A developer moves the unordered case to the front, written as `a == Float.NaN || b == Float.NaN`, so that what follows is a plain three-way comparison. The regression proof against the previous version finds an input with a NaN on which `fcmpl` now pushes 1 instead of -1: a comparison with `Float.NaN` is false for every operand, including NaN.

Tags: [jvm-internals](../README.md#tag-jvm-internals), [interpreter-semantics](../README.md#tag-interpreter-semantics), [numeric-code](../README.md#tag-numeric-code), [special-values](../README.md#tag-special-values)

## The change

Handle the unordered case first, with an explicit test for NaN, and write the rest as `a < b ? -1 : a > b ? 1 : 0`. The old code reached the NaN case by falling through three failed comparisons, which read as an accident; the new code names it. The tests for ordering, -0.0, the infinities and NaN under `fcmpg` all pass.

**Before** ([`Comparison.java`](../../examples/apps/mica/src/main/java/net/terminalvalue/mica/interp/Comparison.java), line 23):

```java
 * equals 0.0, and a NaN is neither less than, equal to, nor greater than anything.
 */
public static int fcmp(float a, float b, boolean nanIsGreater) {
    if (a < b) {
        return -1;
    }
    if (a > b) {
        return 1;
    }
    if (a == b) {
        return 0;
    }
    return nanIsGreater ? 1 : -1;
}

/** {@code dcmpg} when {@code nanIsGreater}, else {@code dcmpl}. */
```

**After:**

```java
 * equals 0.0, and a NaN is neither less than, equal to, nor greater than anything.
 */
public static int fcmp(float a, float b, boolean nanIsGreater) {
    // The unordered case first, so that what follows is a plain three-way comparison.
    if (a == Float.NaN || b == Float.NaN) {
        return nanIsGreater ? 1 : -1;
    }
    return a < b ? -1 : a <= b ? 0 : 1;
}

/** {@code dcmpg} when {@code nanIsGreater}, else {@code dcmpl}. */
```

<details><summary>Patch</summary>

```diff
--- a/examples/apps/mica/src/main/java/net/terminalvalue/mica/interp/Comparison.java
+++ b/examples/apps/mica/src/main/java/net/terminalvalue/mica/interp/Comparison.java
@@ -23,16 +23,11 @@ public final class Comparison {
      * equals 0.0, and a NaN is neither less than, equal to, nor greater than anything.
      */
     public static int fcmp(float a, float b, boolean nanIsGreater) {
-        if (a < b) {
-            return -1;
-        }
-        if (a > b) {
-            return 1;
+        // The unordered case first, so that what follows is a plain three-way comparison.
+        if (a == Float.NaN || b == Float.NaN) {
+            return nanIsGreater ? 1 : -1;
         }
-        if (a == b) {
-            return 0;
-        }
-        return nanIsGreater ? 1 : -1;
+        return a < b ? -1 : a <= b ? 0 : 1;
     }
 
     /** {@code dcmpg} when {@code nanIsGreater}, else {@code dcmpl}. */
```

</details>

## What the verifier found

The two versions disagree. The prover found this input, and the verifier replayed it in jvmcontract's bytecode interpreter against both versions:

| Input | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| `fcmp(a=NaN, b=0.0, nanIsGreater=false)` | `-1` | `1` |

One disagreeing input is enough to fail the build. The domain is `a: float × b: float × nanIsGreater: boolean`; the search tries small values first so that the witness is readable, and would have covered all of it.

## Would the existing tests have caught it?

No: every existing unit test passes (`java -ea net.terminalvalue.mica.Tests`, run against the patched code).

## Why it matters

The two opcodes exist so that javac can compile `a < b` as `fcmpg` and `a > b` as `fcmpl`, each sending a NaN down the false branch; with `fcmpl` answering 1 for a NaN, a guest program's `if (x > y)` with `x` NaN takes the true branch, and `x > y && x < y` can hold at once. Nothing crashes: a sort of floats with a NaN in it comes out in the wrong order, a `Math.max` written by hand returns the wrong operand, a bounds check lets a NaN through. The test with a NaN exercises `fcmpg`, for which the broken check and the fall-through agree; `fcmpl` with a NaN is untested, and `x == Float.NaN` is the comparison Java programmers are warned about in the first chapter on floating point, which is exactly why a reviewer who sees it in a line that says "NaN" in its comment reads past it.

## Why the verdict is right

The regression proof compiles both versions of `fcmp` into one program and asks JBMC for an input on which they differ. Floats are bit-vectors to the solver, NaN among them, and it finds one in the first stage: a NaN operand with the `fcmpl` rule, on which the old code returns -1 and the new code 1, because `a == Float.NaN` is false even when `a` is NaN and the three-way comparison that follows has no case for an unordered pair. The tool replays the input in its interpreter and shows both outcomes. The point of the proof is that it covers every float, NaN and the signed zeros included, where a test covers the values its author thought of.

## What to do

Revert, or write the check as `Float.isNaN(a) || Float.isNaN(b)` (which is `a != a`), and add the `fcmpl` NaN test the regression proof shows was missing. Better: keep the fall-through form, with a comment that the fourth branch is the unordered case, since it is the form in which the specification states the instruction.

## Notes

- `== Float.NaN` is never true, so the NaN check never fires and `fcmpl` quietly becomes `fcmpg`.

## Evidence

How the verdict was reached: found by JBMC 6.11.0 in 0.2 s, replayed in the interpreter; domain a: float × b: float × nanIsGreater: boolean.
